title: Apollo’s flight software was woven by hand, wire by wire
body: The Apollo Guidance Computer kept most of its programs in core rope memory, a read-only memory made of tiny magnetic rings. A wire that passes **through** a ring stores a 1 and a wire that goes around it stores a 0, so the data live in the weaving pattern, not in any magnetic state. The software, written at MIT’s Instrumentation Laboratory, was woven into the ropes by women working in factories, and some programmers nicknamed the result LOL memory, for Little Old Lady memory. With 192 sense wires threading each ring, the Block II computer packed 36,864 words of program into a machine about one cubic foot in size.

slides.alt: Two magnetic cores drawn as rings. One yellow sense wire runs straight through the first ring, storing a 1, then loops around the outside of the second ring, storing a 0.
slides.caption: Through the ring means 1, around it means 0: the program is the weaving.

slides.prompt: With 192 sense wires threading a single core, how much could that one ring hold?
slides.detail: Every wire adds one bit, since it either passes through the core or bypasses it.

slides.label: 16-bit words of woven, read-only memory in the Apollo computer
slides.text: Alongside just 2,048 words of erasable memory. The whole computer weighed 70 lb (32 kg) and held 4,100 integrated-circuit packages.

slides.heading: Apollo’s memory: woven rope next to erasable
slides.note: 16-bit words in the Block II computer: 18 times as much woven program as erasable scratch space.

slides.heading: Why weave?
slides.text: A rope could not be rewritten, which made the program impossible to wipe, and it packed far more into the same space than ordinary core memory. The price: once woven, nothing could be changed.
